title: Fourier Coefficients
body:
The numbers $a_0, a_n, b_n$ in a [[Fourier Series]]. They are **how much of each frequency** the
function contains, and every one of them is an integral:

$$
\begin{dcases}
a_{n} = \frac{1}{\pi} \int_{0}^{2\pi} f(x)\cos(nx)\,dx, \quad n = 0, 1, 2, \dots \\
b_{n} = \frac{1}{\pi} \int_{0}^{2\pi} f(x)\sin(nx)\,dx, \quad n = 1, 2, 3, \dots
\end{dcases}
$$

so that

$$
f(x) \sim \frac{a_{0}}{2} + \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left[a_{n}\cos(nx) + b_{n}\sin(nx)\right]
$$

## Why the integral extracts the coefficient

This is the whole trick and it is [[Orthogonal Functions]] doing the work. Multiply both sides by
$\cos(mx)$ and integrate over one period. Every term on the right dies except one, because

$$
\int_{0}^{2\pi}\cos(nx)\cos(mx)\,dx = \begin{cases} \pi & n = m \\ 0 & n \ne m\end{cases}
\qquad
\int_{0}^{2\pi}\cos(nx)\sin(mx)\,dx = 0
$$

The surviving term is $a_m \pi$, so $a_m = \frac{1}{\pi}\int f(x)\cos(mx)\,dx$. **You are not
solving an infinite system of equations; you are reading off one coordinate at a time**, and the
sines and cosines never interfere because they are mutually orthogonal. Those integrals are
[[Trigonometric Integrals]] from [[CALCULUS 2]], and the ones that are not orthogonality identities
are usually [[Integration By Parts]].

## It is a projection

| Finite-dimensional ([[LINEAR ALGEBRA]]) | Function space (here) |
|---|---|
| $\mathbf{v} = \sum c_i \mathbf{e}_i$ | $f(x) \sim \frac{a_0}{2} + \sum (a_n\cos nx + b_n \sin nx)$ |
| $c_i = \mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{e}_i$ | $a_n = \frac{1}{\pi}\int f \cos nx\,dx$ |
| [[Dot Product]] with a basis vector | [[Inner Product]] with a basis function |
| $\{\mathbf{e}_i\}$ an [[Orthonormal Basis]] | $\{1, \cos nx, \sin nx\}$ an orthogonal family |

A Fourier coefficient **is** a [[Projection]]. The only change from
[[LINEAR ALGEBRA FOR DATA SCIENCE]] is that the sum in the inner product has become an
integral and the basis is infinite. The $\frac{1}{\pi}$ is a normalising constant, present because
$\{1, \cos nx, \sin nx\}$ is orthogonal but not orthonormal.

## Practical facts

- $\frac{a_0}{2}$ is the **average value** of $f$ over the period, the DC offset in signal terms.
  Set $n = 0$ in the $a_n$ formula and see it.
- **If $f$ is even, every $b_n$ is zero.** If $f$ is odd, every $a_n$ is zero, including $a_0$.
  Checking parity first saves half the integrals, and this is the single most useful exam habit
  in the course.
- Over an interval $[0, L]$ rather than $[0, 2\pi]$ the substitution $x = 2\pi t / L$ gives
  $a_n = \frac{2}{L}\int_0^L g(t)\cos\left(\frac{2\pi n t}{L}\right)dt$. That derivation is worked
  in full in [[FOURIER AND COMPLEX ANALYSIS]] under section 2.3.
- In [[Complex Exponential]] form the two families collapse to one coefficient
  $c_n = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi} f(x)e^{-inx}dx$, with $c_n = \frac{a_n - i b_n}{2}$.
- $\sum |c_n|^2$ is the energy of the signal, which is [[Parseval's Identity]].
- Coefficients decay faster for smoother functions. A discontinuous square wave has $b_n \sim 1/n$;
  a continuous triangle wave has $a_n \sim 1/n^2$. **Slow decay is what causes
  [[Gibbs Phenomenon]]**.

## Where else the vault uses this

- [[Partial Differential Equations]] and the [[Wave Equation]] in [[MATHEMATICAL METHODS]]:
  separation of variables produces the modes, and the Fourier coefficients of the initial pluck
  are **how loud each harmonic is**. That is the physical meaning of these numbers.
- [[Discrete Fourier Transform]]: the same coefficients computed from $N$ samples instead of a
  continuous $f$, with the integral replaced by a finite sum.
- [[Orthonormal Basis]] in Linear Algebra for Data Science states the finite-dimensional version of the identical
  argument.
